questions.q: Why do yearly goals often lead to complacency?
a: The deadline feels distant, so urgency fades
The goals are usually too small to matter
People forget them during the summer
They demand too much planning upfront
questions.why: Lesson 1 says a far-off date makes us think we have plenty of time, so effort slips.

questions.q: Which idea from athletes does the 12-week system borrow?
a: Periodization: focused work in shorter stretches
Interval training: bursts of maximum speed
Visualization: rehearsing the outcome daily
Teamwork: sharing every goal with a group
questions.why: Lesson 1 says athletes used periodization first, and the 12-week cycle applies it to goals.

questions.q: What is the difference between lead and lag indicators?
a: Lead indicators are actions; lag indicators are results
Lead indicators are results; lag indicators are actions
Lead indicators are weekly; lag indicators are yearly
Lead indicators are financial; lag indicators are personal
questions.why: Lesson 2 measures ends such as weight lost, and the actions such as running a daily mile.

questions.q: What share of your lead indicator actions should you complete each week?
a: At least 85 percent
At least 50 percent
At least 65 percent
At least 95 percent
questions.why: Lesson 2 says hitting that threshold makes reaching the 12-week goal much more likely.

questions.q: Which three kinds of time block do the authors recommend?
a: Strategic, buffer and breakout
Morning, afternoon and evening
Deep, shallow and social
Planning, doing and reviewing
questions.why: Lesson 3 assigns deep work to strategic blocks, interruptions to buffer blocks, and rest to breakout blocks.
